description: How Rome fought and won an empire — key campaigns, siege tactics and the battle of Actium that changed history.
content_html:
Rome at War

Rome did not acquire its empire by accident. Over five centuries of nearly continuous warfare, the Roman army developed and adapted tactics, organisation and technology that allowed it to defeat opponents as varied as Macedonian phalanxes, Celtic warbands, desert guerrillas and Eastern cavalry. This lesson focuses on Roman warfare in the Imperial period and on two key conflicts: Trajan’s campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century AD, and the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC that determined who would rule the Roman world.

Tactics and Adaptability

The Roman army’s greatest strength was its capacity to adapt. When facing enemies who excelled in archery, Rome recruited auxiliary archers from Syria. When fighting desert nomads, it reorganised supply lines. The fundamental tactical approach, however, was consistent: use the pilum volley to disorder the enemy, close to sword range, and overwhelm with disciplined pressure from the scutum-wall.

Roman generals understood that battle was often decided before it started — by choosing ground, by tiring the enemy, by cutting off supply lines. The logistics of a Roman campaign were extraordinary: granaries at fortresses along the Rhine and Danube, a network of roads that allowed rapid troop movements, and a river fleet that carried supplies deep into enemy territory. Trajan’s Column records this infrastructure vividly — among its carved scenes are soldiers unloading supplies from boats and engineers constructing pontoon bridges.

Key Fact

Trajan fought two major campaigns against the Dacians: the First Dacian War (101–102 AD) and the Second Dacian War (105–106 AD). Both are recorded in detail on Trajan’s Column in Rome and commemorated on the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — two of the most important prescribed visual sources for Roman warfare.

Trajan’s Dacian Campaigns

Dacia, roughly equivalent to modern Romania, was a powerful kingdom north of the Danube ruled by a capable king named Decebalus. Decebalus had humiliated Rome in previous conflicts, extracting tribute money and capturing Roman prisoners. Trajan invaded in 101 AD to recover Roman prestige and to seize Dacian gold reserves that were among the largest in the ancient world. The first war ended with Decebalus surrendering and agreeing to Roman terms; when he broke those terms, Trajan launched a second, more brutal campaign that ended with the destruction of the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa and Decebalus’s suicide rather than capture.

Trajan’s Column, standing in Rome, is a hollow marble column roughly 30 metres tall, around whose shaft winds a continuous carved relief depicting both campaigns in over 150 individual scenes. The column begins with river-gods and troops crossing a pontoon bridge and moves through sieges, battle scenes, negotiations and triumphal processions to the final conquest. The Arch of Trajan at Benevento, a triumphal arch decorated with relief panels, shows Trajan receiving submission from Dacian enemies, distributing grain to Roman citizens, and associating his victories with divine favour. Both monuments present the campaigns as evidence of Roman greatness and Trajan’s exceptional leadership.

Trajan’s Column is an invaluable source for Roman military practice — it shows fort construction, river crossings, artillery use, allied auxiliary troops and siege operations in remarkable detail. However, it was a piece of state propaganda. Trajan is always shown in a commanding position; Roman soldiers are always disciplined and orderly. The Dacians are depicted as brave enemies to make the conquest more impressive, but they are also shown in defeat and submission. The column does not show Roman atrocities, looting or the suffering of civilian populations — it presents an idealised narrative of Roman power. Students must weigh this selectivity when using the column as evidence.

Siege Warfare

Roman success against fortified towns and hillfort strongholds depended on specialised siege techniques. The standard approach involved surrounding the enemy position with a circumvallation — a wall or ditch that encircled the entire position and cut off all resupply. This was then supplemented by direct assault: battering rams mounted in wheeled towers, artillery firing stones and bolts, and approach ramps of earth built up to the level of the enemy walls. Trajan’s Column shows all of these techniques in use against Dacian hillforts.

The Battle of Actium, 31 BC

The naval battle of Actium was fought off the coast of north-western Greece on 2 September 31 BC. On one side was Octavian (the future Augustus) commanding a fleet under his brilliant admiral Marcus Agrippa. On the other were the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII of Egypt. The battle decided who would control the entire Roman world. Octavian’s victory made him undisputed master of Rome and led directly to the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The trireme had been the dominant warship of the classical Greek period, but by Actium the principal warships were larger vessels called quinqueremes and triremes built on a grander scale. Agrippa’s fleet used grappling hooks and boarding tactics to neutralise Antony’s heavier ships. When Cleopatra’s squadron broke off the engagement and retreated towards Egypt, Antony followed — and his remaining fleet, left without leadership, surrendered. The battle showed that naval supremacy could decide the fate of an entire empire.

Key Fact

The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeat the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. The victory is commemorated by a relief in the Vatican Museum and on the shield depicted on the Augustus of Prima Porta statue, where the scene of Actium is carved in miniature on the emperor’s breastplate armour.

The Romans invested enormous effort in commemorating military victory in permanent public form. Triumphal arches — like the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — were built at key road entry points so that every traveller would be reminded of Roman greatness. Victory columns like Trajan’s Column placed the narrative of a campaign literally at the heart of the city, in the forum that bore the emperor’s name. Coins were struck to broadcast the victory to every corner of the empire: the Mark Antony Legionary denarius (minted c. 32 BC) shows a warship on the obverse and an eagle between two military standards on the reverse, advertising his naval and military strength to his soldiers. Even defeat was commemorated: Augustus recovered the eagles lost by Varus in the Teutoburg Forest disaster (9 AD) decades later and displayed them publicly as proof that Rome always demanded and achieved satisfaction.
exam_tip_html: When answering essay questions about Roman warfare and expansion, avoid simply listing battles and dates. The examiner wants you to argue — for example, arguing that engineering was more important than weapons, or that propaganda (Trajan’s Column, the Arch at Benevento) tells us as much about Roman values as about what actually happened. Use named sources as evidence for your argument, not just as decoration. Common pitfall: treating Trajan’s Column as a neutral record rather than as a monument designed to glorify the emperor.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Trajan fought two Dacian campaigns (101–102 AD and 105–106 AD); both are recorded on Trajan’s Column and the Arch of Trajan at Benevento, which are key prescribed visual sources presenting victories as imperial propaganda.
  • The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet defeat Antony and Cleopatra, making Octavian master of the Roman world and leading to the creation of the Roman Empire under Augustus.
  • Roman military success rested on adaptable tactics, engineering capability (camps, siege works, roads) and the political use of commemorative monuments to project Roman power.

practice_questions.text: Name one Roman material source that records Trajan's Dacian campaigns.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Trajan's Column (in Rome); the Arch of Trajan at Benevento.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Romans used siege warfare to capture fortified positions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three: the Romans surrounded the enemy position with a circumvallation to cut off supply; they used battering rams to break down walls; they constructed earth approach ramps up to the level of the enemy walls; artillery (ballistae, onagri) fired bolts and stones; soldiers advanced under protective shelters or using the testudo formation; Trajan's Column records these siege scenes in detail.

practice_questions.text:
Study this description of a Roman monument: a tall hollow marble column, approximately 30 metres high, standing in Rome on a rectangular base. Around its exterior runs a continuous spiral relief carving showing scenes from a military campaign. Among the scenes visible are soldiers crossing a river on a pontoon bridge, legionaries digging ditches and piling up an earthen rampart, artillery machines on platforms being fired at a walled town, and a bare-headed figure in armour addressing troops from a raised platform.

What does this source reveal about Roman warfare? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis linking specific scene types (river crossing, camp-building, artillery, address to troops) to wider knowledge of Roman campaign logistics, engineering and leadership. The response considers the monument's propagandistic purpose — it was built to glorify the emperor and present an idealised version of Roman military values — alongside its genuine informational value. At least two specific details are used analytically with evaluative comment.
Secure: Clear use of specific details with accurate supporting knowledge. Some discussion of purpose or limitations.
Developing: General description of what the source shows; limited analysis.
Emerging: Minimal engagement; knowledge vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the battle of Actium was such an important turning point in Roman history.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: Octavian's victory gave him sole control of the entire Roman world; Antony and Cleopatra's defeat removed the last serious rivals to Octavian's power; Octavian used the victory to justify becoming Augustus, the first Roman emperor; the battle ended decades of civil war that had torn the Roman Republic apart; it established Roman dominance of the Mediterranean sea.

practice_questions.text: How useful is Trajan's Column as a source for understanding Roman military campaigns?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing what the column reveals (engineering, logistics, equipment, formation fighting, siege techniques, allied troops) against its limitations as a propagandistic monument (Trajan always heroic, no Roman atrocities, selective narrative). Named scenes and features are used precisely. The response reaches a supported conclusion about overall usefulness.
Secure: Clear discussion of strengths and limitations with specific reference to the column's content.
Developing: Mainly one-sided; either uncritically accepts the column as evidence or dismisses it without engaging with what it shows.
Emerging: Vague reference to the column; limited accurate knowledge.

practice_questions.text: How effectively did Rome use both military force and propaganda to expand and maintain its empire? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument evaluating both military effectiveness (tactics, engineering, siege warfare, adaptability) and the role of propaganda (Trajan's Column, the Arch at Benevento, coins, triumphal arches) in projecting and consolidating Roman power. The response argues that the two were inseparable — victory was worthless without commemoration, and propaganda without victory was hollow. Named sources are integrated throughout. A supported judgement is reached.
Secure: Clear argument covering both military and propaganda dimensions with relevant evidence. Some range and a supported conclusion.
Developing: Mostly covers one dimension (military or propaganda); limited engagement with the other.
Emerging: Simple points; largely descriptive; evidence thin.

knowledge_checks.q: When was the battle of Actium fought?
Trajan's Column records which of the following campaigns?
options: The battle of Actium against Mark Antony
The conquest of Britain under Claudius
The defeat of Carthage in the Punic Wars

knowledge_checks.q: The Roman practice of encircling an enemy position with a wall to cut off all supply and escape routes was called a _____.
At the battle of Actium, Octavian's fleet was commanded by his admiral _____.
Match each Roman monument to what it commemorates:
right: Trajan's victories and his role as a beneficent ruler

flashcard_questions.q: When did Trajan fight his first Dacian campaign?
What was the Dacian king's name during Trajan's campaigns?
What is Trajan's Column and where does it stand?
flashcard_questions.a: A 30-metre marble column in Rome with a spiral relief recording both Dacian campaigns.

flashcard_questions.q: When and where was the battle of Actium fought?
flashcard_questions.a: 31 BC, off the north-west coast of Greece.

flashcard_questions.q: Who were the two sides at the battle of Actium?
flashcard_questions.a: Octavian (with Marcus Agrippa) against Mark Antony and Cleopatra.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Octavian's victory at Actium lead to?
flashcard_questions.a: He became undisputed ruler of Rome and established the Roman Empire as Augustus.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Arch of Trajan at Benevento?
flashcard_questions.a: A triumphal arch with relief panels depicting Trajan receiving submission and distributing grain.

flashcard_questions.q: What was circumvallation in Roman siege warfare?
flashcard_questions.a: A wall or ditch built around an enemy position to cut off all supply and escape routes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Mark Antony Legionary denarius show on its reverse?
flashcard_questions.a: An eagle between two military standards.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Trajan's Column considered propaganda as well as evidence?
flashcard_questions.a: It presents an idealised narrative glorifying Trajan; Roman failures and atrocities are omitted.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Trajan invade Dacia in 101 AD?
flashcard_questions.a: To recover Roman prestige after earlier humiliations and to seize Dacian gold reserves.

glossary_terms.definition: The art of supplying and maintaining an army in the field; Roman logistical capability was central to the success of long-distance campaigns.
A continuous wall or rampart built by a besieging army around an enemy position to prevent escape and cut off all resupply.
A large warship of the ancient world, propelled by three banks of oars and used for ramming enemy vessels.
